articles.title: US supplies most of the world’s plasma. No country depends on it more than China
articles.summary: The US supplies 70% of the world’s plasma. China’s heavy reliance on its biggest geopolitical rival for this critical ingredient leaves its patients vulnerable.
articles.body: As she watched the pale yellow liquid drip into her mother’s vein, Ge Lan felt the weight of every drop. Her mother, recovering from stomach cancer surgery, relied on daily infusions of human albumin to restore her blood protein levels. At about $46 for a 10-gram bottle, the imported blood product was the costliest medicine in her mother’s treatment. “I just hope (she) gets better soon,” the 44-year-old told CNN. “I’m worried about the money too, but I have no choice.” Over two months, her mother used 72 bottles, costing the equivalent of seven months’ income for Ge, a local store worker in Henan, central China. Without help from her sister, she said she simply couldn’t have afforded the treatment – and without it, her mother’s condition could worsen. China is the world’s biggest consumer of human albumin, the most abundant protein in plasma, which is widely used in care for critical trauma such as burns, and restoring blood protein levels from chronic conditions, like liver diseases. But it’s long suffered a domestic shortfall largely due to strict rules on plasma collection – a legacy of an HIV infection scandal in the 1990s – and it remains heavily reliant on plasma from its biggest geopolitical rival, the United States, for much of its human albumin supply. The US supplies about 70% of global plasma and is one of the few countries that pays donors. Every year, millions of Americans offer up their arms to cover everyday costs – people like 25-year-old Sky Tucker. “While I do know it could save a life, most of the time, I’m just worried about if I’m gonna get my next meal or if I can feed my cats,” said the community college student who sold plasma twice a week for seven years to help make ends meet. More than 60% of China’s albumin market is supplied by foreign manufacturers and all of it is made from plasma collected in the US, according to a 2024 study co-authored by researchers from China’s national and Zhejiang drug inspection authorities. That reliance carries growing risks for Chinese patients. Researchers told CNN that China’s domestic plasma shortfall could leave patients vulnerable to drug shortages and price spikes if US-dominated supply flows are disrupted by geopolitical tensions or global health emergencies, like the Covid-19 pandemic. Beijing appears increasingly aware of that vulnerability. “That’s why they wanted to enhance the capacity of collecting the plasma in the Chinese market,” said Xi Chen, associate professor of Public Health at Yale University. After opening dozens of new licensed plasma collection centers in 2023, the country cleared its first rice-based albumin for market last July, as part of a broader push to reduce reliance on American plasma. Despite the efforts, China still faces an annual shortfall of around 6,000 tons of plasma, according to a CNN calculation based on industry data and estimation of domestic demand cited by Chinese state media. Totally weaning itself off American plasma is deeply complicated for a country still haunted by a 1990s “plasma economy” scandal, where unsafe blood and plasma collection infected tens of thousands of rural residents in central China with HIV. The plasma scandal In the 1990s, local authorities in the impoverished Henan province pinned its economic ambitions on the plasma trade, rallying hundreds of thousands of cash-strapped farmers to sell their plasma, according to archived Chinese state media reports. “Stretch your arm, show your veins; one stretch, one fist — 50 yuan earned,” went the slogan spread widely through villages in central China, according to a 2004 report by The Beijing News, a state-run newspaper. Back then, 50 yuan was roughly equivalent to a month’s income for many rural residents. The frenzy followed Beijing’s decision in the mid-1980s to ban imports of almost all blood products – except human albumin – amid growing fears over the global HIV/AIDS crisis. China sought to build its own plasma-based industry – but the boom ended in catastrophe. The plasma collection spree, found to be rife with unsafe and unsanitary practices such as reused needles, ended up fueling one of China’s worst HIV outbreaks. Henan reported its first HIV case in 1995, prompting local authorities to shut down blood banks across the province. Nine years later, Henan officials admitted 25,000 former plasma sellers in the province had contracted HIV, according to a 2004 official provincial census reported by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV. Independent investigators, including the late doctor and whistleblower Gao Yaojie, argued the actual number could be much higher. Struggle for self-sufficiency The devastating outbreak reshaped China’s blood products industry, prompting sweeping regulations throughout the entire chain from plasma collection to clinical use. It also left a lasting legacy of public distrust. Due to the “bad image” attached to Henan’s “plasma economy,” local governments in Yunnan, Sichuan and Guizhou – mountainous southwestern provinces that followed Henan’s lead in embracing the sector – had been trying to distance themselves from the blood industry, pursuing investments in other fields, according to Yale University’s Chen, drawing on his fieldwork between 2004 and 2017. The stigma from the past scandal still colors public perceptions of plasma donation as “dangerous” today, despite significantly improved safety and regulatory standards, according to a veteran industry executive in China, who talked to CNN on condition of anonymity as they weren’t authorized to speak publicly. Beyond reputational damage, Beijing’s tight regulatory grip over the past three decades – designed to prevent another blood contamination disaster – has also constrained manufacturers’ ability to produce lifesaving medicines, industry analysts say. This concern remained largely under the public radar until a Covid-era crunch thrust it into the spotlight. During the pandemic, plasma-based therapies like human albumin and intravenous immunoglobulin were widely used in treating critical Covid cases in China. A surge in demand then sparked a wave of panic buying, pushing up prices and leaving many patients with chronic conditions struggling to access supplies, according to a representative for a patient community impacted by inherited immune disorders. The person requested anonymity due to the sensitivity in speaking with foreign media. Since that time, calls for self-sufficiency in blood products have grown louder among industry stakeholders, academics, and political advisers – and efforts to address the plasma shortfalls have accelerated. After opening 32 new plasma collection centers in 2023, taking the total number to 302, China’s drug regulator approved the country’s first rice-derived recombinant human albumin, part of leader Xi Jinping’s broader push for China to seize the “commanding heights” in key technologies and industries. Yang Daichang, chairman of the drug’s developer Healthgen Biotechnology, said it’s expected to eventually replace around a quarter of China’s imported plasma-derived albumin, in an interview with state news agency Xinhua. However, the rice-based albumin’s market adoption may be challenging, the veteran Chinese industry source believed, because it can only be used to treat liver cirrhosis – and the cost of production could be comparatively high. If China wants to increase its self-sufficiency, the source believes, the country needs to fundamentally update its decades-old regulatory regime. “China’s regulation of most other products has been getting closer and closer to international standards,” the source said. “But when it comes to blood products, regulation is still lagging far behind… It’s basically stuck at the level of the 1980s and 1990s.” Industry insiders say rules that restrict plasma collection centers to certain geographical areas, and only allow locally registered residents to donate, has left the world’s second-largest population with just 1.5 million to 3 million active plasma donors, according to estimates from Yale University’s Chen. By comparison, the US – with only a quarter of China’s population – has a larger pool of around 4 million, roughly estimated by Peter Jaworski, a professor at Georgetown University who studies the ethics and economics of the plasma business. Why Americans sell plasma China’s tightly constrained plasma industry has stood in contrast to a booming US collection system – propelled in part by financially strained Americans facing soaring prices and a weakening job market – which ultimately underpins China’s imports of human albumin. The number of US plasma centers more than doubled from 601 in 2016 to more than 1,200 last year, according to historical data compiled by Jaworski, who leads the Georgetown Blood and Plasma Research Group. For comparison, that’s roughly the same number of Denny’s restaurants in the US and nearly double the number of Costco stores. The collection volume also jumped from over 35 million liters in 2015 to an estimated 62.5 million liters last year, according to Jaworski. “The industry is growing 6-8% every single year, and it doesn’t look like there’s anything to slow it down over the next 5 to 10 years,” Jaworski added, citing rising global demand for plasma-derived medicines. Michele Goodwin was once part of the American backbone of the $43 billion global industry. The 60-year-old single mother, raising two college students in Northampton, Massachusetts, said plasma provided a temporary lifeline after she left a stable job to pursue a nursing degree, only to find her post-graduation pay was insufficient. Over a year of twice-weekly donations since the autumn of 2023, she earned more than $8,000 before stopping in 2024 because she felt the process was too “time consuming,” “exhausting” and left with her with an “ugly scar” that she didn’t want to worsen. When she was selling plasma to pay the bills, Goodwin said she was too embarrassed to tell anyone. “I didn’t want my kids to know that… I’m literally selling blood from my arm to help put you through school.” Yet she was also grateful for the financial cushion it provided. Those mixed feelings were echoed among over 100 plasma donors Kathleen McLaughlin interviewed for her 2023 book, “Blood Money: The Story of Life, Death, and Profit Inside America’s Blood Industry” – a decade-long investigation into the US plasma industry sparked by her question about where her own life-sustaining medication came from. “Our economy fails people who aren’t wealthy and leads them to take actions that they might not take otherwise,” she said. Most of the people who sell their plasma tend to be under 35, unemployed, without a college degree, Black and male, according to a 2021 study based on two proprietary national surveys conducted between 2018 and 2021. Whether the US paid-plasma industry exploits or alleviates financial hardship remains unsettled in public debate. China also pays plasma donors, but caps donations at every fortnight, up to 24 times a year – far fewer times than the US, where donors can roll up their sleeves up to twice a week, 104 times a year. The World Health Organization advocates for unpaid plasma collection for ethical reasons, arguing in part that it helps protect disadvantaged communities from possible coercion. However, Jaworski, who has donated plasma four times, says payment helps to ensure a sustainable supply of the raw material for lifesaving medicines. For Chinese patients – at least those who can afford the product – the question is less ethical than existential. Until China can produce or replace enough plasma of its own, tens of millions of patients needing human albumin, like Ge’s family, will remain heavily reliant on the vital fluid typically drawn from hard-up Americans. And that reliance begs an uncomfortable question for experts and the author McLaughlin: “If something happens in that country and that system needs to be shut down, where do you get the medication from?”

articles.title: Gas runs dry: Bangladesh factories shut, homes go dark
articles.summary: South Asia News: Bangladeshâs gas crisis has left the countryâs once-busy Ashuganj fertiliser factory silent for more than a year, disrupting fertiliser production, fo.
articles.body: Bangladeshâs gas crisis has left the countryâs once-busy Ashuganj fertiliser factory silent for more than a year, disrupting fertiliser production, forcing industries to cut output and contributing to power shortages and protests over fuel supplies.The state-owned factory, located near the eastern Titas gas field, shut down in March 2025 after a sharp decline in gas production, which was attributed to underinvestment in ageing fields and exploration. The crisis has since been compounded by disruptions to imports from the Middle East amid the US-Iran war.Ashuganj once operated around the clock, using natural gas to produce urea fertiliser for farmers across Bangladesh. The factory employed more than 1,200 people and produced more than 1,000 tonnes of fertiliser a day. It now stands largely idle, with machinery left unused.âOnly the skeleton of the factory remains,â said Md Bazlur Rashid, 59, who spent his entire working life at Ashuganj.âIt has lost its life," he added, as cited by AFP.Ashuganj is among six major urea fertiliser plants in Bangladesh that have either shut down or restricted operations because of gas shortages. Trade union leader Md Abu Kawsar said the shutdowns had cost workers their jobs while putting pressure on an industry closely linked to food security.âYou cannot simply let these factories sit idle and allow them to deteriorate,â Kawsar said. He added that reviving the plants could also help reduce pressure on the countryâs foreign currency reserves.The gas shortage has also spread across Bangladeshâs wider industrial sector. Hundreds of factories, including textile plants, have either reduced production or shut down, affecting an industry that accounts for about 80% of the countryâs export earnings and makes Bangladesh the worldâs second-largest garment exporter.Households have also faced disruptions, with domestic piped-gas supplies frequently cut. Gas-fired power plants are struggling to meet electricity demand, resulting in regular blackouts.The government introduced electricity-saving measures in August, including an order for shopping malls to close one hour earlier, as the gas shortage continued to strain the countryâs energy supply.Electricity generation, industrial units and captive power plants account for more than three-quarters of Bangladeshâs natural gas consumption, leaving households to bear the impact of worsening shortages.Households account for just over a tenth of the countryâs gas consumption but have also faced frequent disruptions. âWe don't get a drop of gas overnight,â said housewife Nargis Begum, 50, who lives near the Ashuganj factory.âThen sometimes the pressure is too low. We can't turn on two burners at the same time.âMany households, particularly in rural areas, have switched to wood-burning stoves, while frequent power cuts have left residents without fans amid sweltering humidity.âThere is no let-up in our suffering,â Begum said. âThere is no guarantee of electricity. It's so hot now. Last night, there were three or four outages.âThe shortages have also triggered protests among gas-powered rickshaw drivers, who have blocked roads after spending hours waiting for fuel.The crisis has been building for years. Bangladesh was largely self-sufficient in natural gas in 2018, but production declined as older fields were depleted while demand continued to rise. The country has increasingly relied on imports, with Qatar emerging as a key supplier.Experts have said successive governments failed to invest sufficiently in gas exploration. Energy Minister Iqbal Hasan Mahmud Tuku blamed the previous government of Sheikh Hasina, which was ousted in a 2024 revolution, for failing to drill new wells.âThe previous government stayed away from gas exploration,â he told an energy security conference in Dhaka in July. âOur dependence on imports has brought us to this point.âCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Pakistan News: Pakistan minister Ahsan Iqbal has said India could âweaponiseâ the Indus Water Treaty (IWT) and expressed hope that âbetter senseâ would prevail to pr.
articles.body: Pakistan minister Ahsan Iqbal has said India could âweaponiseâ the Indus Water Treaty (IWT) and expressed hope that âbetter senseâ would prevail to prevent the two neighbours from going to war again, this time over water.He noted that the treaty had remained âuntouchableâ for almost seven decades since it was signed in 1960, but New Delhi has now been kept in abeyance âunilaterally."â...Indus Water Treaty that has stood the test of time for the last 70 years. India and Pakistan fought several wars, but it (IWT) was considered untouchable because it is an international agreement, and this time around the Indian government has unilaterally held it in abeyance... first time probably water has been weaponised in history,â Iqbal told the Asia Society.âWe (Pakistan) now face this threat that they (India) can use water as a weapon to deny Pakistan when it needs it for its crops and release it when we don't need it... We are using all the diplomatic means to make sure that we don't have future wars on water because we have already seen lots of wars,â the minister added.He further stated that South Asian countries should instead focus on issues such as development, poverty, illiteracy and the youth âbulgeâ, describing the region as the âleast integratedâ in the world."So we hope that there is better sense in our neighbour's (India) mind and we don't see that water is weaponised and we go to another conflict with India over water because Pakistan cannot surrender at any cost the future of its 250 million people for its food security and right of water. If we let it happen, then every state that is on the lower side of water supply would be hostage to any country that controls the rivers," the Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz) leader remarked.Iqbal's remarks came days after Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif warned India of a âdirect responseâ for putting the IWT in abeyance.âIndia proved itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. I declare in clear terms that every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. If India does not come to its senses, it will be responded to directly,â Sharif said on August 13, on the eve of Pakistan's Independence Day.New Delhi put the agreement in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year. Since then, Pakistani leaders have repeatedly called water their âred lineâ and threatened India over the move, describing it as an âact of war.âCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Saltash man completes 2,800 mile scoot across Australia
articles.summary: Bob Brown from Saltash has ridden a non-electric scooter from Perth to Sydney.
articles.body:
A man has completed a challenge to cross the width of Australia on a non-electric kick scooter.

Bob Brown from Saltash, Cornwall started his journey in July and travelled about 2,800 miles (4506km) from Perth to Sydney, where he finished his trip on Monday.

He said he hoped to break two Guinness World Records - to become the fastest person to cross the country on a kick scooter, while also being the first to travel the route by three different methods, running, cycling, and scootering.

Brown said "after a lifetime packed with adventure, at 57-years-old I wanted another epic adventure before I got too old".

Brown's is no stranger to the country and hoped to raise £5,000 for three charities - MacMillan Cancer Support, St Luke's Hospice and Children's Hospice South West.

In 2001 be became the first Briton to run across the country covering 3,000 miles (4828.032km) in 60 days, before in 2003 he cycled the route becoming the first person to have both run and cycled across Australia.

"I wanted to raise awareness of the need for youngsters to get off their screens and devices and to seek out adventure", he said.

He said he got injured while completing the challenge.

"On day five my wing mirror got clipped by a passing vehicle and I skidded onto the hard shoulder" but was "relatively unscathed".

"Also on the last day, with just 20km to go, I had a serious fall when my handlebars broke going down a steep hill", he added.

Despite the complications, Brown completed the challenge in 31 days, four hours and 10 minutes.

He said he had submitted his documentation to Guinness but had to wait to see if the organisation would officially recognise his achievements.

articles.title: Move to honour Channel Island journalists who resisted occupation
articles.summary: A commemoration is planned to journalists who resisted Nazi occupation during World War Two.
articles.body:
A memorial is planned to Channel Islands journalists who resisted Nazi occupation during World War Two.

The journalists included Joseph Gillingham and Joseph Tierney who were arrested, deported and died in prison for sharing news heard on banned radios and Frank Falla, who survived imprisonment and whose book The Silent War tells how islanders outmanoeuvred censorship.

The appeal by the Chartered Institute of Journalists for a plaque, in the journalists' church St Bride's in Fleet Street, London, has been led by historian Timothy Crook and has already reached its £1,000 target.

Crook said a "memorial can contribute to the restoration of a missing chapter of British journalistic history".

German armed forces occupied the Channel Islands from June 1940 until May 1945. While the islands' civil governments remained in place under German oversight, laws were introduced to confiscate and ban radios, enforce curfews and made everyone carry ID cards.

Crook said: "The memorial plaque intends to pay tribute to the people who spread news during the occupation by illegally listening to the BBC news having retained their radio sets after the order for their confiscation in June 1942.

"They distributed the BBC news they heard verbally or through clandestine news sheets.

"Many were not journalists before the occupation, but they certainly became courageous journalists during the occupation by disseminating the BBC news in these ways."

Institute president Gerald Bowey said donations received meant there could be a commemoration "to acknowledge the outstanding efforts and bravery of Channel Islands residents and journalists to resist censorship and keep the news flowing".

What happened in the Channel Islands during WW2?

The concrete reminders of five years of occupation

The appeal follows a talk to the institute by Cambridge University academic Gilly Carr, who spent a decade searching archives around the world to uncover information about the fate of Joe Gillingham from Guernsey and Joe Tierney from Jersey.

Gillingham was one of five members of the Guernsey Underground News Service (GUNS) who were deported and imprisoned for wireless offences and secretly spreading news.

GUNS was a loose collection of people who secretly listened to the BBC news, wrote it down and shared it with other islanders.

Often the news would contradict that put out through island newspapers, which were only allowed to carry war news provided and approved by the German authorities.

Carr's research resulted in the 2016 BBC documentary Finding Our Fathers , which followed the discovery of where Gillingham and Tierney had been buried in Europe.

Both men were crammed into cattle trucks and sent to prisons in the heart of Nazi Germany but their fates remained a mystery for 70 years.

Carr took the daughters of Gillingham and Tierney to Europe to retrace their fathers' steps in the hope of finding clues and eventually found their graves.

The St Bride's memorial could help extend Frank Falla's own campaign for recognitionl which involved writing letters to ministries and newspapers long after the war ended.

Falla fought for compensation for his fellow former political prisoners in the Channel Islands and, in 2010, his daughter gave Carr her father's extensive archives .

Carr, who described the files as "the single most important resistance archive ever to emerge from the Channel Islands" ensured it became available online.

The fundraisers said they hoped the memorial plaque would be placed in the south aisle of the church.

articles.title: It’s ‘Black August’ in Russia, but Putin is sweeping this summer’s crisis under the rug
articles.summary: “Black August,” or “the August curse,” has become a sort of journalistic shorthand in Russia for dramatic crises that seem to happen in the last weeks of summer. But amid the uneasy speculation this year, Putin has projected his usual aura of confidence.
articles.body: Over the past few decades, “Black August,” or “the August curse,” has become a sort of journalistic shorthand in Russia for dramatic crises that seem to happen in the last weeks of summer. In some respects, Black August is Russia’s rough equivalent to the “silly season” in British journalism, the late-summer lull when frivolous headlines seem to dominate while parliament is out of session and royals are on holiday – or announce surprise returns home. But Russian folk wisdom is more pessimistic: a scan of recent Russian history appears to support the belief that dramatic, Black Swan events do tend to strike in August. Thirty-five years ago, a group of Communist hardliners led a failed putsch against Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, unleashing the centrifugal forces that ultimately led to the collapse of the Soviet Union. In August 1998, a financial crisis hit Russia, causing a default on domestic debt and a collapse of the ruble. And one year later, a group of militants led an incursion into the southern Russian republic of Dagestan, kicking off the second Chechen War, a conflict that launched a political unknown, a former KGB officer named Vladimir Putin, into the top echelon of power. Putin became Russian leader on New Year’s Eve of 1999, after a surprise handover by President Boris Yeltsin. But the new tough-guy leader was not immune from the August Curse either. One of his first major tests in office was the sinking of the Kursk, a nuclear submarine that went down with 118 sailors on board. And in August 2008, Russia went to war with neighboring Georgia, showing the belligerent new face of Putin’s foreign policy. The past summer in Russia has also been shaping up as a bleak season for Putin’s Russia. Progress on the contested front lines in Ukraine by Russian troops has been scant; the skies over Russian cities have been blackened by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and Amazon-style distribution centers; and long lines at the fuel pumps and rumors of a fresh wave of mobilization have Russians grumbling. Is this another Black August? Exiled Russian commentator Ilya Varlamov posted his thoughts on that question this week, saying recurring historical disasters in August were “a coincidence, of course.” But, Varlamov continued, “many Russians await August with apprehension. Especially now, when the country is truly in crisis. … The fuel crisis has returned, prices are rising and have no intention of stopping, the ruble is falling, elections are coming and God knows what else.” Varlamov also noted the recently publicized remarks made by a top Russian economist, who warned that Moscow was facing a “social crisis” and “losing both the technological and economic competition globally” and would not win a war of attrition against a Ukraine backed by the West. Even loyal, pro-Kremlin tabloid Moskovsky Komsomolets noted the traditional August anxieties in Russia, though it turned to astrology for guidance. “A lunar eclipse is set to occur this month; while not the most massive one, it will take place opposite Pluto – a planet associated with catastrophes,” the article read. “This could trigger social shifts, political changes in relations with neighbors, and domestic unrest. Incidents of accidents, heightened anxiety, and breakdowns – including nervous disorders – may increase.” But amid the uneasy speculation, Putin has projected his usual aura of confidence. In remarks Wednesday on infrastructure and development projects, the Kremlin leader acknowledged the economic damage inflicted by Ukraine by strikes on the warehouses of e-commerce giant Wildberries, without naming the company – but downplayed their long-term impact. “It goes without saying that these attacks will not have, do not cause and cannot bring about any critical consequences,” he said. “True, they do cause harm – this much is obvious, and we understand this, we see this, and we are aware of it.” The Russian president said those logistics facilities would be built back with government support. But the war in Ukraine has been coming ever closer to home for many Russians, hitting them squarely in the pocketbooks. Ukraine is also weathering domestic crisis in wartime. Earlier this week, recently ousted Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for wartime elections, presenting a fresh political challenge to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Whatever the merits of Fedorov’s arguments, the move potentially presents a fresh talking point to Putin, who has publicly and repeatedly cast doubt on Zelensky’s legitimacy as president. Therein lies the contrast. Zelensky’s five-year term was originally expected to end in 2024, but elections in Ukraine have been postponed under martial law imposed following Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. And the government reshuffles in Kyiv, as well as major anti-government protests, show that civil society and democratic processes are still alive and well in Ukraine. The same can hardly be said for Russia. On Monday, a court in that country convicted opposition politician Lev Shlosberg to 11 years in prison for opposing the war in Ukraine. Russia’s Supreme Court also barred Shlosberg’s party, Yabloko, from appearing on the ballot in upcoming parliamentary elections. Russia’s domestic political opposition, then, has been effectively throttled since Putin launched his war on Ukraine. As the American author Ernest Hemingway would doubtless recognize, the stifling of civil society seemed to happen slowly, then all at once with the death of jailed opposition leader Alexey Navalny in February 2024. Navalny’s fatal journey to an Arctic prison colony also began on an August day in 2020, when he fell ill from nerve-agent poisoning on a return flight to Moscow from Siberia. Coincidence or not, the month of August has been a punishing one for Russia.

articles.title: Man leaves tired 7-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji during family hike
articles.summary: A man who left his tired 7-year-old son to wait alone on Japan’s Mount Fuji while he continued a family hike has been reprimanded by police.
articles.body: A man who left his tired 7-year-old son to wait alone on Japan’s Mount Fuji while he continued a family hike has been reprimanded by police. The boy was spotted sitting on his own at a hut about 8,200 feet (2,500 meters) above sea level – slightly more than halfway up the country’s tallest mountain – by a worker on Thursday, according to CNN’s affiliate TV Asahi. The case was then reported to the police. Police said the boy had gone hiking with his father and older brother and was told to wait there when he became “tired” and reluctant to continue walking, TV Asahi reported. He was told to wait on a bench at the sixth station of the Fujinomiya trail as his father and brother continued their ascent, the report said. When they returned five hours later, police were waiting with the young boy, who was unharmed and handed back to his father. The officers warned the man he could be held criminally liable, the Japanese TV broadcaster reported, adding that he expressed his remorse. Climbers of the 12,388 feet-tall (3,776 meters) volcano have had to be rescued after suffering altitude sickness in the past. Weather conditions up the mountain can also be unpredictable. Authorities have introduced new rules in recent years, including a cap on the maximum number of climbers per day and requiring them to take a brief class about hiking safety.

articles.body: National Security Advisor Ajit Doval is set to arrive in Beijing on Monday for the 25th round of India-China Special Representatives talks on the boundary issue with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi.The talks are scheduled to take place on Tuesday, according to official sources, as cited by PTI.The talks come ahead of the expected visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12-13.While Beijing has not officially confirmed Xiâs participation, officials on both sides remain optimistic that he will attend, potentially opening the way for a meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi to discuss steps to advance bilateral ties.Doval and Wang serve as the designated Special Representatives for the boundary talks mechanism, established in 2003 to seek a comprehensive resolution to the India-China border dispute, which stretches 3,488 km.Although the mechanism has not resolved the boundary dispute, officials on both sides consider it a useful platform for managing recurring tensions and addressing differences between the two countries.Doval and Wang last met in August 2025 on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin.Ahead of the upcoming talks in Beijing, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Saturday reiterated that peace and tranquillity along the border are essential for maintaining good relations between India and China.External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said earlier this month that India views issues concerning the border areas with China as âmost seriousâ and stressed that maintaining peace and tranquillity along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) is of âutmost importanceâ. He said the situation along the frontier would determine the overall trajectory of India-China relations.New Delhi had earlier rejected Beijingâs criticism of Indiaâs decision to assign official names to 27 places and geographical features in Arunachal Pradesh, asserting that the state is an âinalienable and integralâ part of India and that nothing can change this âindisputable realityâ.China, which claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of South Tibet, has issued its own set of names for places in the region since 2017.India has dismissed the practice as âvain and preposterousâ, maintaining that such actions cannot alter the âundeniableâ reality that Arunachal Pradesh âwas, is, and willâ always remain an integral part of India.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Hindu family of four found dead in locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur; strangulation suspected
articles.summary: South Asia News: Four members of a Hindu family, including a retired schoolteacher, were found dead inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city under suspici.
articles.body: Four members of a Hindu family, including a retired schoolteacher, were found dead inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city under suspicious circumstances, with police investigation under way, as per ANI citing local media.The bodies of Ganapati Chakraborty, 65, his wife Pritilata, 50, their daughter Agami, 23, and their 12-year-old son Priyam were recovered from their home in the Daspara (Machhuapara) area around 11.30pm on Saturday, police said, suspecting strangulation and robbery in inital probe.The bodies were found in different parts of the house. Ganapatiâs body was recovered from the roof, those of his wife and daughter from the staircase, and Priyamâs body from under a bed, according to Subir Chowdhury, in-charge of Rangpur Metropolitan CID.âThe household belongings were found scattered and in disarray. For now, it appears to be a robbery. However, nothing can be confirmed until the investigation is completed,â Chowdhury said, as quoted by Bangladesh local The Daily Star.Meanwhile, Sanatan Chakrabarty, deputy commissioner of Rangpur Metropolitan Police and head of the Detective Branch, said the victims were initially suspected to have been strangled. The bodies were sent to Rangpur Medical College Hospital for autopsies, while police, CID and Detective Branch teams launched a joint investigation.The family had not been heard from since Thursday. Pritilataâs sister Puja Chakraborty told The Daily Star that all four phones had been switched off since Thursday night.âWe came to Daspara on Saturday night after finding their phones switched off. The main gate of the house was locked and all the lights inside were off. Police later arrived, broke the lock and entered the house, where they recovered the bodies,â she said.Ganapati had retired from Rangpur Zilla School in December last year and had since been working as a homeopathic practitioner. His daughter had completed a masterâs degree in English, while his son was a Class 5 student.The family had lived in the area for about four years and Ganapati had built the three-storey house, although construction was still incomplete, locals said.Rangpur police commissioner Mohammad Abdul Mabud said the investigation was being treated as a priority. âWe will know how they died once we receive the autopsy reports,â he said.The deaths come amid continued concern over attacks and violence involving Bangladeshâs Hindu minority. Human Rights Watch has reported attacks on Hindu homes, while minority groups have documented a broader pattern of violence against religious minorities. However, there is currently no evidence as of now establishing that the Rangpur killings were communal or linked to the victimsâ religion.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Power protests erupted across several parts of Karachi as residents took to the streets over prolonged and unannounced outages, blocking major roads and burning tyres while demanding restoration of electricity.Demonstrations were reported in Pak Colony, Liaquatabad, Gharibabad, Nishtar Road, Bhimpura and Ranchore Line, disrupting traffic across key parts of Pakistanâs commercial capital. In Liaquatabad, protesters blocked major intersections, while clashes between traders and K-Electric (KE) staff over outages escalated into tyre-burning on Nishtar Road, as reported by local news outle Dawn.Residents said they were facing 12 hours or more of daily power cuts, often without adequate notice. The outages have also disrupted water supplies as pumping stations remain shut when electricity is unavailable, adding to public anger.âBill-paying citizens are being punished with 12-hour load-shedding,â a protester in Liaquatabad said.The crisis also hit businesses and households, with residents reporting spoiled food, disrupted studies and sleepless nights as fans remained unusable during blackouts.The protests compounded an already severe traffic situation in the city. Roads were also closed for traditional Chup Tazia processions, while the power protests triggered additional blockades. Traffic police diverted vehicles to alternative routes, but those too became congested.Asif Khan, a private-sector employee, told Dawn he took four hours to travel from SITE to Liaquatabad after leaving work around 5pm. Another commuter said an ambulance carrying his feverish mother was stuck for about two hours near Civic Centre while they were travelling to a doctor in Saddar.âWe pay bills on time but still face 12-hour power outages. articles.title: In 1995, a retired British bus driver began covering his modest home with empty beer containers; around 75,000 cans later, it was known as the Can House
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover the story of the Can House in Hartlepool, a unique folk art site created by Philip Muspratt using 75,000 beer cans. Explore its history, impact on the community, and legacy after its demolition.
articles.body: What began as an unremarkable project became the Can House, one of Englandâs most unusual folk art sites, in Hartlepool. Philip Muspratt was born in 1952 and passed away in 2015. Between his birth and death, he served in the armed forces as well as being employed as a bus driver until his early retirement due to a disability, as recorded in the SPACES Archives entry on the Can House and noted in local obituaries describing him as a retired bus driver who died aged 63. The project began as a simple gesture of kindness, not as a work of art. This began when Muspratt decided to decorate his back garden with found materials to cheer his elderly father, who was deaf and unable to speak.The Can House, an entry from the SPACES Archives, a nonprofit organization that documents self-taught art environments, describes how the project's true starting point came when Muspratt noticed piles of empty beer bottles left behind by his son and his son's friends. So he decided to construct a wall from them in his back garden, a construction that reached two layers of bottles in width, five feet in height, and approximately 23 feet in length, which took him five months to build, as described in the SPACES Archives entry on the Can House. The same entry reports that Musprattâs son was struggling with alcoholism, giving him a steady supply of used bottles for the project.From bottles to cansThe project switched materials around 2005. After learning that his son had switched to drinking from cans, Muspratt began collecting cans instead. His hobby quickly became more serious: he aimed to keep decorating the property with empties and raise money to restore a local war memorial through scrap metal sales. People around Muspratt heard about the project and began sending him bags of empty cans.A landmark and a filmThe Can House became more than just a curiosity for one individual. It attracted visitors from outside Hartlepool, including some from America, and became a social hub after many nearby pubs had closed. RIP the Can House, a Cultural Landmark Made from Empty Beer Cans, a retrospective published by Vice, describes how filmmaker Maxy Bianco spent time documenting life inside the house for a 52âminute film first screened in 2012 and later shared online, which drew more than 20,000 views and a screening at Londonâs Floating Cinema in Hackney Wick. The Vice article notes that Muspratt had started covering the semiâdetached house in 2005, eventually layering on more than 75,000 beer cans in intricate patterns, including a fully functioning can fountain in the back garden. Biancoâs 52âminute documentary follows not just the house but Muspratt, his wife Sue, and their children and grandchildren, capturing both the communal drinking and the toll of daily alcohol abuse.The Vice story also sheds light on the complexities that were involved in building this colorful home. Biancoâs documentary showed both the sense of community the project created and the reality of the alcohol addiction behind its materials. According to Kevin McGrother, a local musician who recorded a video inside the house, Muspratt initially started to collect the cans to pay for the renovation of the memorial at the church, as quoted in Viceâs retrospective âRIP the Can House, a Cultural Landmark Made from Empty Beer Cans.End of the Can HouseMuspratt died in 2015, leaving the house deserted for several years after nearly two decades of decoration. The property was demolished as part of a larger redevelopment plan for Hartlepoolâs Dyke House area. The housing association Thirteen acquired the house as part of the Willow Fields redevelopment, which aimed to replace several prewar houses with 64 two- and three-bedroom homes. The demolition process started in 2018, and the entire house was torn down later that year, as reported in local news coverage of the Can Houseâs removal. Although the structure no longer stands, the Can House remains a notable example of vernacular art in Hartlepool. It joins other self-made art environments created by people without formal art training and reflects the roles of grief, addiction, and community in the project.Such details have since led to the site being recorded by archives and outsider art scholars as an extraordinary beer-can landscape within Western Europe: 75,000-odd cans neatly structured across facade and yard. In this instance, one of the SPACES Archives entries has the Can House listed with a host of other vernacular art environments; an example of how Muspratt converted a humble semi to an informally visited local landmark. And although the structure can no longer be visited, traces of its post-industrial creative spark survive in a wealth of photographs, news clippings and video shorts still appearing online.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Where water conflicts pose the biggest threat in 2026
articles.summary: Water-related conflicts have nearly quadrupled since 2020. As World Water Week 2026 begins, Al Jazeera unpacks the data.
articles.body:
The sharp rise in water-related conflicts in recent years is in focus as the World Water Week conference begins on Sunday in Sweden’s capital, Stockholm, and online.

With the theme “Water for People and Progress”, the conference is organised annually by the Stockholm International Water Institute (SIWI) and highlights growing global water-security challenges.

According to the Pacific Institute, a US-based nonprofit water think tank, 420 water-related conflicts were recorded in 2024 – a record high and a 78 percent increase from the 235 conflicts recorded in 2022.

The increase is largely driven by attacks on water infrastructure and disputes over access, particularly in regions affected by prolonged wars.

For more than three decades, the Pacific Institute has tracked global water conflicts through its Water Conflict Chronology, classifying each incident by whether water served as a casualty, trigger, or weapon of war.

Casualty: Water infrastructure is damaged or destroyed during conflict, either deliberately or as collateral damage. This can include dams, pipelines, wells, treatment plants and power systems needed to maintain water supplies. In 2024, 55 percent of water-related conflicts were driven by casualty events.

Trigger: Water scarcity, unequal access, or disputes over resources fuel violence, often involving communities, farmers, animal herders, or armed groups. Scarcity and access disputes remain widespread, with 28 percent acting as triggers for water-related conflicts in 2024.

Weapon: Water is deliberately manipulated to harm or pressure opponents, including by cutting supplies, contaminating sources, flooding areas, or controlling access. Water weaponisation is less frequent but persistent, underscoring the growing links between water stress, climate pressures and conflict, with two percent of incidents in 2024 categorised this way.

In Gaza, 1.9 million of 2.1 million people remain displaced, while about 90 percent of water and sanitation infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed by Israeli attacks, according to UNICEF.

Up to 70 percent cannot collect the minimum six litres of water per person a day for drinking and cooking and 90 percent of households faced moderate-to-high water insecurity.

The medical charity, Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), also known as Doctors Without Borders, reported that water prices have risen by up to 500 percent. Repeated attacks, restrictions on supplies and damage to water facilities have disrupted distribution, worsening diarrhoeal and skin diseases and increasing risks for children and pregnant women, MSF added.

In the occupied West Bank, settler attacks and Israeli demolitions have damaged and destroyed Palestinian water infrastructure, with repeated raids on the Ein Samiya wells east of Ramallah cutting supply to about 100,000 people.

Since April 2023, fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces has displaced about 12 million people and created a humanitarian crisis affecting more than 30 million.

A Geneva Academy report documented attacks on water infrastructure, including reservoirs, treatment plants and distribution networks, particularly in Darfur. The collapse of water and sanitation systems has fuelled cholera outbreaks and worsened food insecurity, with famine risks rising across Darfur, Kordofan and Blue Nile.

US and Israeli air strikes on Iran since February 28, have further strained a water system already weakened by years of drought, below-average rainfall, depleted groundwater and agricultural demand.

Attacks reportedly damaged desalination plants and reservoirs in Qeshm Island and Hormozgan province, disrupting water supplies to tens of thousands of people. Damage to electricity networks and roads has hindered repairs. The attacks came as Iran’s reserves were critically low, with some reservoirs up to 92 percent depleted. Water levels in reservoirs in Mashhad, Iran’s second-largest city and home to around four million people, dropped below three percent.

The war on Iran has exposed the vulnerability of critical water infrastructure in a region that is among the most water-scarce in the world.

Across the Gulf, water security depends heavily on large desalination plants to convert seawater. They supply about 90 percent of drinking water in Kuwait, 86 percent in Oman and 70 percent in Saudi Arabia. In Bahrain, it is above 90 percent and in Qatar, 99 percent.

Desalination plants were damaged in Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE and Iran during the war, though the reported impact on water supplies was largely limited.

Ukraine’s water crisis has worsened as the war with Russia damages vital water and energy infrastructure. UNICEF says 4.3 million people received safe-water assistance last year, while 12.7 million need humanitarian support.

Attacks have reduced electricity generation by 70 percent, disrupting water and heating. In Kherson, strikes this month cut supplies to entire neighbourhoods.

The Kakhovka Dam disaster in June 2023 affected more than 100,000 people, while about 10 million now lack reliable access to safe water.

articles.title: Hormuz crisis hides a deeper oil threat that could outlast the war
articles.summary: Art Berman warns that 8 million barrels shut in near the Strait of Hormuz may never fully recover, even after a ceasefire reopens the waterway.
articles.body: As global attention remains fixed on tankers moving through the Strait of Hormuz, a petroleum geologist is warning that the more consequential energy story may be unfolding thousands of feet underground — and could continue long after any political agreement ends the fighting. Art Berman, a petroleum geologist and energy consultant with more than four decades of industry experience, told Fox News Digital that millions of barrels of Persian Gulf oil production remain shut in and warned that restoring those wells is far more complicated than simply reopening the strategic waterway. "This is potentially a kind of a world-changing event, even if we resolve the political issues," Berman said. "The bigger story and the more important one long term is that 8 million barrels of Persian Gulf production is currently shut in and world production is down about 10 million barrels a day," Berman explained. IRAN TURNS TO PUTIN AS US TALKS COLLAPSE, HORMUZ STANDOFF THREATENS GLOBAL OIL FLOW "We can move tankers around and we can obsess about, you know, are there 4 million barrels getting through or are there 6 million or 9 million or whatever the right number is," he added. "But eventually, those tankers have to be filled with oil." A White House official, speaking on background, pointed to the sharp decline in oil prices following the signing of the MOU and said the Strait of Hormuz is open, with the U.S. naval blockade in full effect. Berman's estimate of Gulf shut-ins is broadly consistent with the latest assessment from the International Energy Agency. The IEA said in its Aug. 12, 2026, Oil Market Report, "Gulf oil production rose by a further 2.5 mb/d in July to 23.9 mb/d, still 8.3 mb/d below pre-war levels." Global oil supply remained 6.3 million bpd below year-earlier levels, according to the agency. The U.S. Energy Information Administration offers a somewhat different estimate. EIA assessed production shut-ins at an average 5.5 million bpd in July, while warning that continuing constraints on Hormuz transit had forced the agency to increase its forecast for shut-in production in August. EIA expects production and trade patterns to generally return to pre-conflict conditions in early 2027, but says some Gulf producers may not regain their previous output during its forecast period. TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA ‘Not like turning on a switch’ The distinction is important because much of the public discussion has centered on what the industry calls the midstream problem — whether tankers can safely transport oil through Hormuz — while Berman argues that the upstream problem of producing the oil itself could prove more enduring. "The very last thing in the world I ever want to do is to shut in a well," Berman told Fox News Digital. Restarting a well requires restoring communication between equipment at the surface and reservoirs thousands of feet underground, he explained, and extended shutdowns can create complications inside the reservoir and well. "This is not like turning on a switch for a light bulb," Berman said. "It's a complicated, high-risk, relatively long-term process, and we don't know the outcome." Berman estimated that roughly 80% of affected wells could return close to their previous production levels, although he said that could take weeks or months. He said many of the remainder could require additional engineering work and some could ultimately produce at lower rates. "Some of that production will never come back," he predicted. Other energy analysts agree that restarting Gulf production presents substantial technical challenges. But Wood Mackenzie is more optimistic than Berman about the ultimate recovery. Its analysis projects that fields affected by the Hormuz closure could return to approximately 70% of their previous production within three months and 90% within six months, assuming a controlled restart. The final roughly 1 million bpd could take considerably longer. CHINA ORDERS FIRMS TO IGNORE US IRAN SANCTIONS, DARING US TO ENFORCE CRACKDOWN Berman also warned against assuming that a ceasefire or political agreement would immediately restore pre-war energy flows. Shipowners, insurers and crews would first have to become confident that tankers could safely navigate the waterway, while other logistical and security issues could continue even after governments reached an agreement. "A simple political agreement doesn't mean the problem's over," Berman said. ‘A world-changing event’ Berman's argument goes considerably further than predicting a slow oil-market recovery. He contends that the Persian Gulf conflict represents a fundamental shock to the global energy and economic system — one whose consequences will persist even after the immediate crisis ends. Asked about his comparison with the COVID-19 pandemic, Berman told Fox News Digital that the scale of oil production affected by the current crisis makes it comparable to the largest economic disruptions of recent years. "This is not just a news cycle," Berman said. "This is potentially a kind of a world-changing event, even if we resolve the political issues." IRAN DEAL CLOCK HITS ZERO AS TRUMP DEMANDS ‘WHITE FLAG’ WITH NEW PRESSURE CAMPAIGN LOOMING Why Americans are not insulated The United States is the world's largest oil producer, but Berman argues that does not isolate American consumers from the disruption. "The oil market and the refined products market is global," he told Fox News Digital. Berman noted that U.S. refineries require different grades of crude to produce the country's mix of gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other petroleum products, meaning domestic production alone cannot eliminate America's exposure to international markets. "The problem for the U.S. isn't that we don't have enough oil, we almost do," Berman said. "It's that the oil we have isn't the right kind" for everything American refineries produce. EIA reported July 15 that Hormuz disruptions had already pushed international buyers toward alternative sources of petroleum products, contributing to higher U.S. refinery margins, production and exports. Whether that recovery proceeds as EIA expects or encounters the technical obstacles Berman warns about could determine how long the economic consequences of the conflict linger after the shooting stops. For Berman, the question is no longer simply when tankers return to Hormuz. It is whether the global energy system that emerges afterward will ever operate quite the way it did before. The White House pushed back on concerns that the disruption represents a lasting threat to U.S. energy security, pointing to record American production and blaming Iran for instability in the critical shipping corridor. "Thanks to President Trump, the United States is now the world’s number-one producer and exporter of oil and gas. Record oil and gas production strengthens our energy independence and national security," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital. "The Iranian regime’s terrorist actions in the Strait of Hormuz have proven that our allies need to invest in reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources and advance new partnerships with the United States that enhance the world’s energy security," Rogers added. articles.title: Your Significant Other May Be 'Cushioning' And You Wouldn't Even Know It
articles.summary: The behavior is also known as "backburnering."
articles.body:
Years ago, writer Sara C. felt palpable chemistry with a coworker. She had been married for 14 years at the time, but her friendship with the man was flirtatious and she started to fixate on it. They communicated regularly and had coffee dates. Then they slept together.

But a line was crossed even before the physical relationship began: Sara had invested in a figment of a relationship until it became a real one, to the detriment of her marriage.

Relationship: Too Many Couples Believe These 'Myths' About Healthy Relationships

"My affair definitely started out as an emotional affair ," said Sara, whose last name has been withheld to protect her privacy. "I think many people in steady relationships sometimes stagnate or get into tiffs that remain unresolved."

"Whether it's boredom or complacency or unresolved frustration, I'm not sure," she added. "But it makes them see other people in a different light and can elevate the human connection."

Those lingering connections are sometimes called backburner relationships . A "backburner" is "a person to whom one is not presently committed, and with whom one maintains some degree of communication, in order to keep or establish the possibility of future romantic and/or ****** involvement," according to a 2014 study in Computers in Human Behavior .

The concept has also been called "cushioning" ― as in, " I have a Plan B ready to cushion the blow if Meg and I don't work out ."

Relationship: 7 Sneaky Signs Of Resentment In Relationships

It's more than just a "what-if" situation, though. Backburner relationships require relatively frequent communication, Jayson Dibble, the 2014 study's lead author and an assistant professor of communication at Hope College, told The Atlantic at the time .

These affairs of the heart ― and of the imagination ― make sense from an evolutionary standpoint: If the goal is to have as many options as possible for reproduction, the occasional Instagram "like" and "wanna get coffee?" text is easy enough to maintain. At the same time, you ensure your future offspring will have someone to care for them by staying with your partner.

Marriage and family therapist Elisabeth LaMotte likens cushioning to a "pre-meditated version of rebounding."

Cushioning typically indicates an inability to exist without a relationship, she said. And more often than not, our backburner fulfills (or seems to fulfill) something that's missing in our primary relationship.

Relationship: You Might Be A 'Burned-Out Pursuer' In Your Relationship. Here's What That Means.

"With cushioning, you're usually cultivating a secret flirtation with someone who represents an exaggerated rebellion against challenges in one's current relationship. For example, someone who is dating a successful but anxious partner might cushion with a relaxed partner who is unable to keep a job," she said. "But cushioning denies both parties a chance to see if the anxiousness (or any other challenges) might be lessened through communication and effort with our primary partners."

We imagine the grass is greener on the other side ― and in the process, we short-shrift what very well may be a solid relationship. Once pursued, backburner relationships are subject to the same frustrating, everyday complications any other couple experiences.

Sometimes, the relationship peters out quickly or forces you to grapple with your own unresolved issues. This was the case for comedian and writer Xaxier Toby . Six years ago, Toby pursued a relationship with a friend of a friend he'd always had " If only I were single... " thoughts about.

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost .

"I'd just been dumped and instead of dealing with that, I leaped straight to the backburner," said Toby, who has written a number of comedy books including Mining My Own Business .

"It didn't go anywhere, of course, and just delayed me dealing with the pain of a breakup, with the bonus of unfairly messing with someone and involving them in the emotional mess that was me at that time," he added.

Relationship: In Defense Of Getting Back Together With Your Ex (Yes, Seriously)

Toby said he now understands why backburner relationships are so common.

"They provide a little jolt of validation that you might be missing in your relationship due to turmoil, but that's all they'll ever be," he said. "They're like sugar. Instantly gratifying, addictive, but without any nutritional value."

Cushioning is unfair to both your current partner and the person acting as your cushion, said Samantha Burns , a dating coach and the author of Breaking Up & Bouncing Back . They're also unhealthy for you.

"Cushioning stems from a place of insecurity, or underlying feelings of dissatisfaction in your current relationship," she said. "If you're cushioning, ask yourself why you need the outside attention and validation. Is it making up for some needs that are not being met in your relationship? Is it distracting you from acknowledging that you're unhappy or disconnected from your partner?"

Take your time if you need it. But if you realize you want to refocus on your primary relationship, do so with intentionality.

"When you're more insightful and mindful about your thoughts and feelings, you can figure out if you want to remain in your relationship and communicate with your partner instead of going outside the boundaries of your relationship," Burns said. "Successful couples turn inwards, not outwards."

The original version of this story was published on HuffPost at an earlier date.

articles.title: Israel’s war on Gaza forces Palestinians to rely on ‘Stone Age’ toilets
articles.summary: The displaced in Gaza are struggling to find safe, discreet and sanitary toilets amid health crisis.
articles.body:
Deir Al-Balah, Gaza – Eman Mahmoud Shamia has been uprooted several times since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, before finally settling into a new home – a tent in a camp.

It provides rudimentary shelter for 33-year-old Eman, her husband, Yahya Shamia, 50, and their five children, all under 11, but it lacks many of the basic amenities her old home provided.

With the help of a worker who specialised in digging soakaway underground drainage pits, the community in the camp built a “municipal toilet”. It provides relief b ut Shamia said it reminds her of the Stone Age.

There is little in the way of privacy, particularly for women and children, and for some it is difficult to use or access, particularly for her husband, who suffers from an advanced stage of lung cancer.

“I am deprived of my basic right to have a proper toilet seat in my tent. This is exhausting for me as a woman and a mother of five children and my husband is sick and unable to use the makeshift toilet. What is happening to us is madness,” Shamia told Al Jazeera.

“I cannot believe this is our situation. Sometimes I feel like I am going crazy. How did the toilet become like this and how did the door become just a piece of cloth?”

While hundreds of thousands have lost their homes in Gaza, often overlooked are the daily struggles the displaced face in maintaining some level of dignity in their tent towns. The primitive communal toilets they often rely on are an example.

The ongoing Israeli siege has seen the price of sanitation supplies shoot up with a used toilet seat now costing between 1,500 ($503) and 2,000 shekels ($671).

Due to unaffordable prices, Palestinians are making their own primitive toilets by cutting holes into plastic chairs with a layer of sand underneath.

Mohammad Al-Hanouti, 30, from Al-Bureij refugee camp, has an unstable income from his small streetside stall and lives in an unfinished apartment without proper plumbing. What little he earns, he puts towards a toilet.

“I will live without tiles, without a kitchen and without a proper toilet… I have been saving to buy a toilet seat because it is the most important thing in the apartment. Honestly, I am in trouble – getting the basic necessities will cost me around $2,000,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The crisis over toilet seats needs to be addressed urgently. I am not the only one suffering from this; I have friends in the tents who are also struggling.”

He said proper toilet access is a “most basic right” and called on international organisations to import toilets and distribute them in Gaza to those in need for free.

Economist Omar Salouha said the toilet crisis is the result of a “severe supply shock” caused by restrictions on importing toilets, sanitation supplies and plumbing materials.

With more than nine in ten Palestinians in Gaza displaced and over 90 percent of homes damaged or destroyed during the war, there has been a massive increase in demand for toilet products.

“The huge imbalance between supply and demand has caused the prices of used toilets to increase several times over and created a market suffering from scarcity and distortion,” Salouha says.

Some Palestinians are using the rubble of their destroyed homes to make toilets, but Omar says that is not a low-cost option, with seats becoming “a monopoly commodity”.

This means that communal toilets are the only option for most in Gaza, with a single toilet being used by 20 or 25 people.

“There are usually no separate facilities for men and women… [making toilet access in Gaza] a daily necessity linked to health, privacy and dignity”, said Omar.

These facilities often lack proper sinks and taps, so residents use water hoses or barrels of water. Hand sanitiser and toilet paper have become “luxuries”, he added.

In some areas of Gaza, water is only available once a week and many of the camps lack integrated sewage networks, forcing residents to dig pits next to communal toilets to dispose of wastewater.

Hossam Al-Huwaity, spokesperson for the Chamber of Commerce, said it is encouraging traders to submit formal import requests to bring in essential sanitation supplies to help cope with the crisis.

The chamber has also called on UNICEF, the World Food Programme, OCHA, the European Union and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) organisations to help. But, the main obstacle remains the Israeli blockade on Gaza, he said.

“Most commercial requests and appeals remain stuck due to unjustified restrictions and delays at the crossings,” Al-Huwaity added.

A WASH assessment by the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) found that only half of people surveyed in Gaza had access to basic sanitation. Around 60% were exposed to wastewater or human waste within 10 metres of where they lived, contributing to the spread of diseases.

Dr Ahmed Al-Jedi, an emergency department physician at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in Deir al-Balah, said large numbers of children, women and older people are arriving at the emergency department with recurring cases of diarrhoea, skin diseases or gastrointestinal problems.

“Many of these cases are linked to the difficult living conditions inside the tents, where there are not enough facilities for bathing and personal hygiene, and some families may only be able to bathe once a week,” he said.

“Children spend long hours outside the tents because of the heat, playing in the sand, while the same limited space is used for eating, drinking and sleeping, and in some cases toilets are located very close to living areas.”

"It’s the best evidence that the communists who try to get to power in democratic nations are scam artists," Ferrer said. "Fidel Castro and Hugo Chávez denied what they were until they had secured power." RNC WARNS DEMOCRATS FACE 'POLITICAL SUICIDE' AFTER DSA PRAISES FIDEL CASTRO, DEMANDS RUBIO'S PROSECUTION Castro denied being a communist before consolidating power for himself. Before the Bolivarian Revolution, they had an apartment, steady work, and an ordinary middle-class life. Then the promises were replaced by empty shelves and government rationing. Milk disappeared from stores. Meat became scarce. The government assigned citizens shopping days and required them to scan their fingerprints before determining what they were allowed to purchase. This is how communist control enters daily life. It doesn’t always begin with soldiers in the streets. Sometimes, it’s just a few regulations at the grocery store. SOCIALISM WILL 'CONTROL PEOPLE' AND 'TAKE EVERYTHING AWAY' FROM AMERICA, ACCORDING TO THESE EXPATS "The common denominator is that they destroy free enterprise," Di Martino said. "You cannot start a business, you cannot feed your family, therefore you die, or you flee." When the state controls food, employment and housing, citizens lose the ability to provide for themselves without bureaucrats' permission. The government does not need to imprison every dissident. It can seize your paycheck, apartment or your next meal. People who depend on the state for sustenance live at the will and convenience of their captor. SEN TOM COTTON: DEMOCRATS SAY SOCIALISM WILL HELP. HISTORY SAYS IT WILL HURT Communism doesn’t just control your physical necessities. Mike Gonzalez shared how it wages war on faith, conscience and independent thought. As a child in Cuba in the 1970s, he was harassed for attending church and pressured to join the communist Pioneers. Regime thugs interrogated him at age 11. Communism’s advocates respond to witnesses like Ferrer by reaching for an excuse. "Because they tried to control the message." EXPERT WHO FLED CUBA WARNS OF ‘VICIOUS CYCLE’ THAT WILL LEAD TO ‘COMMUNISTS IN DOUBLE DIGITS’ IN CONGRESS Faith, family and national traditions remind people that the state is neither the source of truth nor the highest object of devotion. That is why communist movements teach citizens to despise their country. Its history becomes irredeemable, its traditions oppressive and its culture illegitimate. Once people are convinced that their institutions are rotten, destroying them can be sold as an act of liberation. PASTOR FREED FROM CHINESE PRISON AFTER TRUMP RAISED HIS CASE WITH XI JINPING Pastor Ezra Jin experienced what happens when a regime decides that even faith itself is a threat, after he and 20 other church leaders were arrested in China just last year. The Chinese Constitution formally promises religious freedom, but the Communist Party places itself above the Constitution. Jin was eventually released, but eight of his fellow pastors remain behind bars. Their only crime was worshipping something other than the party. His story exposes the emptiness of rights that exist only on paper. A constitution offers no protection when the ruling party recognizes no authority above itself. Use whatever Marxist label you want; every variation uses the same blueprint. Discredit the institutions that limit its authority. Subjugate economic freedom, education, religion and public speech. articles.title: A tiny owl flew 70 miles out to sea and collapsed on a yacht, exhausted and too weak to fly, she found an unlikely group of rescuers who refused to leave her behind
articles.summary: Europe News: A British Army sailing crew got recently an unexpected passenger during a race around Britain and Ireland when an exhausted barn owl landed on their b.
articles.body: A British Army sailing crew got recently an unexpected passenger during a race around Britain and Ireland when an exhausted barn owl landed on their boat about 70 nautical miles from shore.The bird was found struggling in the open sea on Thursday while the crew of Fujitsu British Soldier was taking part in the 50th Anniversary RORC Round Britain and Ireland Race. According to Reuters, the sailors saw the owl fall into the water several times before it finally managed to reach the boat.The exhausted bird then collapsed on the deck. The crew secured it with a towel and began looking after it as they continued towards the finish line at Cowes. They later named the owl Little Reg, before changing the name to Little Regina.The Barn Owl Trust, Marine and Wildlife Rescue and Caister Independent Lifeboat also became involved in getting the bird safely back to shore while the Army Sailing Association crew continued the race.Owl kept trying to reach boatAccording to Sergeant Mark Petherbridge of 2nd Battalion, The Parachute Regiment, the bird tried to get onto the boat after falling from the mast and into the sea. "We thought we'd lost her, but she kept fighting her way back up and to the boat," Petherbridge said.The bird had reportedly tried to land on the head of one of the crew members before tumbling into the water. It fell into the sea three times before eventually making it onto the deck.Once aboard, the sailors realised that the owl was extremely tired. Skipper Will Naylor told race officials that the crew now had an additional member for the latter part of the race."We have an extra crew member for the latter parts of the race. An exhausted barn owl that we are nursing back to health," Naylor said. He also joked about the unusual addition to the crew, saying, "Someone is going to have to walk the plank!"The sailors continued to care for the owl as their boat made its way towards Cowes. The race covered 1,805 nautical miles, and the crew could not simply stop their journey to take the bird back to land.Wildlife groups pitch inAs the sailors continued their journey, arrangements were made to get the owl off the racing boat and back to land. The Barn Owl Trust, Marine and Wildlife Rescue and Caister Independent Lifeboat helped with the rescue. The lifeboat collected the bird so it could be taken to a wildlife centre for further care.The owl was eventually transferred to the RSPCA East Winch Wildlife Centre in King's Lynn, England. Staff at the centre said the bird was in poor condition when it arrived."The owl is sadly very emaciated and weak, but is now receiving fluids, nutrition, warmth and plenty of rest. We are doing our best to help it," the centre said in a Friday update, People's Magazine reported.The wildlife centre also asked people to donate items that could help with the owl's recovery, including heavy-duty cat beds.James Stannard, a conservation officer for the Barn Owl Trust, helped organise resources after receiving a call about the bird. He told the BBC that the owl had little access to food while it was on the racing boat and could have died without being taken back to land.Stannard also offered a possible explanation for how the owl ended up so far from shore. He believes the bird may have unknowingly roosted on a fishing vessel while it was docked. If that vessel later went out to sea, the owl could have been carried into open water without realising it. He described the bird's ability to find another boat as "nothing short of a miracle".The race began from the Royal Yacht Squadron in Cowes on August 9. It attracted 33 boats and 182 crew members representing 22 countries. Johnny Vincent's Volvo 70 Pace later edged out Palanad 4 on corrected time to win the overall IRC victory.
